rules.name: public_items_are_documented
rules.description:
Every public function, struct, enum, and module has a doc comment
explaining its purpose.

rules.name: description_yields_clear_verdict
rules.description:
Every lint rule's `description` states one unambiguous property whose truth
is the verdict — written as a plain invariant naming just the condition for
the property to hold, and spelling out the violating case only when it adds
detail the positive statement leaves unclear (such as concrete examples).
False when a description leaves the judge to infer which verdict a clause
maps to, naming the failing case in prose ("is a violation", "is not
allowed", "should be avoided", "is discouraged") instead of the direct
`false when <condition>`, or when its holding and violating conditions
overlap.

rules.name: name_describes_what_the_rule_checks
rules.description:
Every lint rule `name` is a descriptive identifier that conveys the property
its `description` checks — a meaningful token, never a placeholder or nonsense
one (for example rule1, foo, bar, baz, test, todo, asdf, temp, thing, xxx),
that names the same thing the description evaluates.

rules.name: relevance_scopes_conditional_rules
rules.description:
A lint rule that only applies in some situations expresses that with a
`relevance:` condition rather than an inline applicability clause in its
`description` (for example "or not applicable", "if present", "when
relevant"), keeping the verdict a clean pass/fail.

rules.name: path_scoped_rules_use_files_not_relevance
rules.description:
A lint rule that applies only to a subset of files identifiable by path — a
file type or extension (for example only `*.py`) or a location or directory
(for example only files under `src/`) — declares that subset with `files`
globs rather than a `relevance:` condition, since a path scope is
deterministic and spends no judge tokens; `relevance` is reserved for
conditions on a file's content or changes that a glob cannot express.

rules.name: description_omits_already_excluded_situations
rules.description:
A lint rule's `description` specifies behavior only for situations the rule
actually evaluates, never stating a property, exception, or caveat for a case
its own `relevance:` condition or `files` scope already excludes (for example
a rule scoped by `files` to `*.py` adding "for Python files" or "non-Python
files are exempt", or one whose `relevance` gates a condition that the
description then repeats) — the excluded case never reaches the judge, so the
redundant clause only spends tokens and blurs the verdict.

rules.name: relevance_scopes_without_deciding_the_verdict
rules.description:
A lint rule's `relevance` condition decides when the rule is judged, not how
it comes out: among the files it admits, the `description` can still land
either true or false. False when a `relevance` asserts the checked property
itself (so every admitted file passes) or names exactly the violating case
(so every admitted file fails) — for example
`relevance: the file defines a function with no docstring` under
`description: every function has a docstring`.

rules.name: description_and_relevance_are_concise
rules.description:
Every rule's `description` and any `relevance` condition state their point in
the fewest words that keep the verdict unambiguous — no filler, no restating
the inverse, no narrative beyond the check. A judge call batches an agent's
rules into one prompt, so tokens one rule wastes degrade the judge on the
others; extra length is warranted only when it adds clarity the shorter form
lacks, such as concrete examples or easily-confused edge cases.

rules.name: line_localizable_rules_require_attribution
rules.description:
A lint rule sets `require_line_attribution: true` exactly when every violation
its `description` permits can be pinned to specific line(s) containing the
concrete offending token, statement, directive, comment, declaration, or config
key, and omits the field when a violation is inherently cross-cutting and cannot
be pinned to one source line, such as agreement across files or a whole-file or
architectural property.

rules.name: handlers_delegate_to_services
rules.description: Request handlers delegate business logic to a service layer.

rules.name: modules_have_doc_comments
rules.description: Every module begins with a doc comment explaining its purpose.

rules.name: errors_are_contextualized
rules.description: Every returned error adds context about the operation that failed.
rules.relevance: the change adds or modifies error handling

rules.name: no_todo_without_ticket
rules.description: No TODO comment without a tracking ticket reference.

rules.name: no_inline_sql
rules.description: All database access goes through the query builder, never inline SQL.

rules.name: always
rules.description: A positive invariant

rules.name: conditional
rules.description: A positive invariant
rules.relevance: When Rust files exist

rules.name: comments_earn_their_place
rules.description:
true when every code comment in the target files earns its place: it explains
something the code does not make obvious — intent, a non-obvious constraint, a
tradeoff, a subtle "why" — and does so tersely. false when a comment restates
what the adjacent code plainly says or narrates mechanics a reader can see
(`# increment i`, `// loop over users`, `# return the result`), is a decorative
section banner or divider that adds no information, is dead weight (commented-out
code, a stale TODO with no owner or context, changelog or session notes left in
the source), is verbose where a short phrase would do, or reproduces explanatory
content already covered by a reference it links (or that the file links elsewhere)
instead of keeping just the repo-specific "why" and deferring the rest to that
reference — a copy that both bloats the comment and silently drifts from its
source. A docstring or comment that documents a public contract, an example, or a
genuinely non-obvious rule is NOT a violation even if longer.
rules.relevance: the target files contain code comments

rules.name: e2e_not_mocked
rules.description:
true when every end-to-end or integration test in the target files drives the
real artifact across real boundaries (the entry point as a subprocess, real
temp files, a real local server or database). false when any such test mocks
the network, filesystem, subprocess, or the entry point it is meant to exercise.
rules.relevance: the target files define an end-to-end or integration test

rules.name: tests_mirror_real_usage
rules.description:
true when every end-to-end or integration test in the target files exercises
the software through the same interface its real users use — invoking the real
entry point (a CLI as a command, an HTTP route as a request, a public API as a
caller, a UI through user-facing actions like click/type/navigate) with
realistic inputs, and asserting on user-observable outcomes. false when a test
reaches past that interface to take a shortcut a real user could not: calling
private internals, firing synthetic events, driving component handlers
directly, or mutating internal state to reach a condition only the interface
should produce.
rules.relevance: the target files define an end-to-end or integration test

rules.name: changed_behavior_has_e2e
rules.description:
true when EVERY distinct behavior these changes ADD or MODIFY is exercised
by a real end-to-end or integration test — each new or altered code path,
output, exit status, and failure/recovery path, not one happy-path test standing in for the whole change — and every
behavior they REMOVE has had its obsolete end-to-end test removed with it.
Where the cheapest honest end-to-end proof would cost more than the defect
it prevents, a deterministic structural assertion satisfies this rule,
provided that assertion states at its own site why the end-to-end proof was
declined.
Locate the tests for this entry point or module — read the repo's test tree
as needed — and confirm coverage by an existing or new test, or by the
justified structural assertion above. false when an assertion lacks that
reason, any added or modified behavior lacks proof, or a removed behavior
retains an obsolete test.
rules.relevance:
the target files add, alter, or remove observable behavior and BOTH criteria
hold. Judge only those changed paths, not pre-existing, untouched behavior:
(1) The behavior is authored in this repository. A guarantee a third-party
tool makes in isolation belongs to that tool's maintainers: clippy failing
on its own finding, a formatter reformatting, or a package manager refusing
an unlocked dependency. What this repository composes out of tools into a
path of its own is authored here and tested by nobody else — which artifacts
get published and where, what an installer writes and starts, or what a
script does around the tool it calls. A structural claim is excluded even
when authored here: it is settled by reading a file rather than running
anything. Whether a gate recipe invokes every tier the policy declares is
proved by a deterministic check reading the recipe; running the gate proves
it more slowly and no better. Apply this criterion rather than matching a
list; the examples illustrate its reach, not its limits.
(2) The failure would otherwise be silent. Ask what happens if this behavior
breaks and nothing tests it. A release or publication path shipping a broken
artifact is discovered by whoever installs it; a deployment or provisioning
script, a scheduled job, and a developer tool that checks something are
discovered late or never. Those failures are silent and owe end-to-end proof.
A quality gate that stops refusing bad code is loud — the first red change
that merges says so — as is a build that stops building or an entry point
that stops running. Apply this criterion rather than matching a list; it
reaches equally a silent failure none of these examples names.
A test is not itself the behavior under test, and a behavior-preserving edit
(a refactor, formatting, a comment, docs, configuration, or a type-only
change) that no user could observe does not meet the criterion.

rules.name: tests_assert_real_behavior
rules.description:
when every test in the target files asserts on an observable outcome (a
returned value, an exit code, persisted state) rather than exercising code
without asserting any behavior.
rules.relevance: the target files define tests

rules.name: names_match_behavior
rules.description:
true when every name the target files declare describes what it actually is or
does at the breadth it claims: a broad name (`process`, `data`, `utils`, `--all`)
covers everything it implies or is narrowed to its real job, a specific name does
exactly that. false when a name overclaims its breadth, hides a side effect, or
contradicts what its value or body does.
rules.relevance: the target files declare a named variable, function, command, flag, type, module, or file

rules.name: suppressions_justified
rules.description:
when every comment-style linter or type-checker suppression directive and every
in-language type-system escape hatch in the target files carries a brief reason
why it is necessary. Such suppressions include Python `Any`, `cast`, and
`# type: ignore`; TypeScript `any`, `as`/`as any`, non-null `!`,
`@ts-ignore`, and `@ts-expect-error`; Go `interface{}`/`any` and unchecked type
assertions; and directives such as `# noqa`, `eslint-disable`, and Rust
`#[allow(...)]`. These examples are illustrative, not exhaustive: justified
uses at genuinely dynamic or deserialization boundaries comply, while
unjustified uses are findings.
rules.relevance: the target files contain a linter or type-checker suppression directive or an in-language type-system escape hatch

rules.name: boundary_inputs_validated
rules.description:
when every external or IO input read in the target files (request bodies,
environment variables, config files, third-party responses, CLI arguments,
stdin) is validated at the boundary before use.
rules.relevance: the target files read external or IO input

rules.name: no_hardcoded_secrets
rules.description:
when every secret the target files rely on — a credential, API key, access token,
connection string, or private key — is read from an environment variable or a
secret store by name rather than embedded as an inline literal.
rules.relevance: the target files handle credentials, connect to a service, or hold configuration

rules.name: least_privilege_grants
rules.description:
when every access grant in the target files (a CI token's `permissions:`, an agent
command allowlist, a cloud IAM policy, a database role, an OAuth scope) is scoped to
the minimum the work needs — no write access where read suffices, no wildcard
permission, no unbounded allowlist.
rules.relevance: the target files grant a permission, token scope, role, or command allowlist

rules.name: diagnostics_error_or_absent
rules.description:
true when the quality gate treats every diagnostic as a hard failure — no
linter, type checker, or compiler is configured to emit warning-level output.
false when any check is left warning-only.
rules.relevance: the target files configure a linter, type checker, or compiler

rules.name: tool_output_is_signal
rules.description:
Judges the output a repository's OWN code produces — the lines its scripts,
functions, and recipe bodies print themselves.
true when every script or command recipe in the target files is quiet on
success (a single line or nothing) and, on failure, prints the exact error
plus a concrete next action; a body that only hands work to a build
orchestrator, task runner, package manager, or test runner (`nx affected`,
`uv sync`, `pytest`) is true whatever that tool prints, which the repo
neither owns nor should silence.
false when a script's or recipe's own output is noisy on success, or when it
fails with a message that omits the cause or the fix — including a delegated
command's failure that it swallows or reports without either.
rules.relevance: the target files define a script or command recipe

rules.name: agents_md_durable_and_terse
rules.description:
true when each durable instruction file in the target files (AGENTS.md,
CLAUDE.md, and a skill's SKILL.md) reads as durable, terse instructions —
constraints, tradeoffs, and judgment a future maintainer or agent needs. false
when any reads as a session or changelog narrative, or restates what a command,
a failing gate, or a linked doc already shows.

rules.name: no_redundant_instruction_pointers
rules.description:
The agent harness auto-loads every AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md colocated with or in an
ancestor of the files in scope, and any markdown doc reachable from one of those by
following reference links — directly, or nested through other docs — is thereby
surfaced to the reader as already available to load. This rule judges the files in
that set. true when the target file does not redirect the reader to read, see, or
consult another file already present in the same context — a colocated or containing
AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md (auto-loaded up the tree), or a doc already loaded or already
advertised upstream on the reference path that reached this file (e.g. a referenced
doc pointing back at the parent that linked it). false when it defers content to, or
tells the reader to go read, such an already-present file as if it were not already
available: dead weight that silently rots when the target moves or is renamed.
Introducing a genuinely new resource — one not already reachable in the current
context — is fine, as is a plain note about a file's role (e.g. that CLAUDE.md is a
symlink of AGENTS.md).
rules.relevance:
the target file is an AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, or a markdown doc reachable from one by
following reference links (directly or nested through other docs) — i.e. a file the
agent already loads automatically or has been prompted it can load; skip markdown no
AGENTS.md reaches

rules.name: new_code_lands_in_a_project
rules.description:
Every repo is laid out as an Nx project graph, so nothing runs outside it.
true when the file belongs to a project the graph already declares (the nearest
project definition covers its path), or the change declares that project
itself. false when it lands at a path no project definition covers, so Nx can
neither run nor skip it and the work escapes `affected` entirely.
rules.relevance: the change adds the file rather than editing one that already exists

rules.name: work_goes_through_command_surface
rules.description:
true when docs, CI workflows, and scripts invoke build, test, lint, format, or
setup work through the project's documented command surface (its `just`/task
recipes) rather than re-implementing the underlying commands inline. false when a
workflow, doc, or script hand-rolls the raw command a recipe already wraps, so the
two drift and the recipe stops being the single place that defines the behavior.
rules.relevance: the target files run a build, test, lint, format, or setup step that a documented recipe already wraps

rules.name: contracts_have_one_source_or_a_drift_gate
rules.description:
true when the restatement is anchored to one authoritative source:
derived from it by codegen, with the output checked in and its freshness
gated, or reconciled against it by a check in the quality gate that fails
on drift. false when only convention holds the restatement and its
original together, so the two diverge silently the next time either side
changes.
rules.relevance:
the target files restate a value, type, schema, column, key, field, or
enum that is also declared across a contract seam — any agreement two or
more parties must both hold to where at least one side can change
independently of the other. Apply that criterion rather than matching a
list: it is met by a call or transport surface (an HTTP route, a method
signature, a CLI flag schema, an event payload), by a persistence or
storage schema and the data model behind it (a table and its columns, a
document or key shape, an on-disk or wire format, a cache or queue entry,
a store shared across a boundary), and by an interface between internal
collections of code (what a package, module, or library owns and what
another may assume of it) alike, and equally by a store, serialization, or
internal boundary none of those examples names. A duplicated literal or
constant list, a re-declared field, column, or key set, and a parallel type
beside the original are restatements; reading, calling, importing from, or
annotating against a data model or an internal module is not

rules.name: project_graph_is_present
rules.description:
true when the repo declares an Nx project graph — an `nx.json` at the root
plus project definitions covering its work.

rules.name: session_bootstrap_provisions_toolchain
rules.description:
true when the session bootstrap makes a fresh web/cloud session able to run
the `just` command surface with no manual step: a `SessionStart` hook in
`.claude/settings.json` runs an idempotent, non-blocking
`scripts/session-setup.sh` that ensures `just` itself — a cloud image often
ships the language runtime but not `just`, and there is no asdf there to read
`.tool-versions`, so the first `just ...` call would otherwise fail — before
handing off to any llmlint installer. false when the hook is absent, points
at a script that never provisions `just` (leaving the recipes unrunnable), or
the provisioner is not idempotent / does not skip when `CI` is set.
rules.relevance: the repo automates session setup via a Claude Code SessionStart hook

rules.name: gate_runs_every_stage
rules.description:
true when `just check` composes the FULL gate for this stack — format check,
lint, type check (where the language has one), unit tests, AND e2e — each an
actually-invoked command. false when a stage the stack needs is missing from
`check` (e.g. type checking or e2e is defined as a recipe but never reached by
`check`), so the gate passes while a whole class of defect goes unchecked.

rules.name: coverage_gate_actually_fails
rules.description:
true when the test command in the gate both measures coverage and FAILS the
build below the threshold — a real `--cov-fail-under`, `coverageThreshold`,
`--fail-under-lines`, or equivalent enforcing flag. false when coverage is
only reported (printed, uploaded) without a failing threshold, or the
threshold is commented out.
rules.relevance: the repo enforces coverage in-gate rather than documenting an opt-out in AGENTS.md

rules.name: upgrade_refreshes_and_gates
rules.description:
true when `just upgrade` (or the equivalent recipe) upgrades dependencies to
their latest allowed versions AND re-runs the full gate, so a fresh repo lands
on current deps proven green. false when `upgrade` only bumps a lockfile
without re-running `check`, or no upgrade path exists at all.

rules.name: dependencies_upgraded_to_latest
rules.description:
true when the committed lockfile is on the latest versions the repo's declared
constraints allow; false when any dependency is behind a newer version reachable
within its constraint and no committed file records why it is held back (a
rationale in AGENTS.md, or a comment on the pin / lock entry). A fresh repo must
land on current deps, and the `upgrade` recipe merely existing (see
`upgrade_refreshes_and_gates`) does not prove it ran — so verify behaviorally by
running the stack's read-only dependency-staleness check (a dry-run upgrade or an
`outdated` listing) and reading what it reports.
rules.relevance:
the repo declares and locks third-party dependencies (a dependency manifest
plus a committed lockfile the staleness check can read)

rules.name: no_secret_committed_in_tree
rules.description:
true when no credential, API key, access token, connection string, or private
key is committed anywhere in the tree — every secret is referenced by name from
an environment variable or secret store. false when any real secret value is
embedded in a committed file.
rules.relevance: the target file could hold a credential, token, key, or connection string

rules.name: ci_runs_the_real_gate
rules.description:
true when CI bootstraps a clean checkout and runs the full `just check` gate.
false when CI omits the gate or runs only a reduced subset of it.

rules.name: ci_llmlint_job_provisions_a_runnable_harness
rules.description:
true when the CI job running the llmlint tier installs a harness the repo's
`oneharness.toml` fallback list names (e.g. codex, or claude-code) onto PATH
before the lint step — `setup-llmlint.sh` installs `llmlint` + `oneharness`
but no harness. false when the job wires only the harness credential (e.g.
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`): oneharness then finds no harness, skips every file,
and the job passes while linting nothing.
rules.relevance: the repo runs the llmlint LLM-judge tier as a CI check

rules.name: install_path_matches_docs
rules.description:
when the CI end-user install job installs the artifact via the exact command the
README documents.
rules.relevance: the repository ships an installable artifact

rules.name: pr_gate_runs_the_affected_tier
rules.description:
true when the pull-request gate job runs the affected tier — the repo's gate
recipe delegating to `nx affected` keyed off an explicitly derived merge base
(`nx-set-shas`, or an explicit `--base` computed from `git merge-base`). false
when the PR gate sweeps every project with `run-many`, or leaves the base for Nx
to infer, which a shallow CI checkout makes non-deterministic.

rules.name: broader_sweep_runs_at_exactly_one_lifecycle_point
rules.description:
true when exactly one job runs the broader-tier full sweep, placed where the
repo's release model puts it: at merge-to-main when the merged commit is the
commit that ships, or at release-prep when releases are batched behind a release
PR or a manual cut.

rules.name: required_checks_name_only_pr_context_jobs
rules.description:
true when every context named is a job that reports on a pull request — the
affected-tier gate, the PR-title lint, the llmlint tier. false when the
broader-tier sweep, or any other job that runs only after merge or at
release-prep, is named.
rules.relevance: the target files record the repo's required status-check contexts

rules.name: console_entry_point
rules.description:
true when the CLI is declared as a `project.scripts` entry point in its own
project's `pyproject.toml` (the uv workspace member that owns the command,
not the workspace-root manifest), so it installs as a real command. false
when the CLI is only runnable via `python -m` with no console entry point
declared, or the entry point is declared on a manifest that does not ship
the command's code.

rules.name: supply_chain_gate
rules.description:
when `cargo deny` and `cargo machete` run as a dedicated CI job and a `deny.toml`
is committed.

rules.name: binary_e2e_is_its_own_crate
rules.description:
true when that suite lives in its own `publish = false` Cargo workspace
member holding only `tests/`, declared as its own project whose `test`
target depends on the binary crate's `build`, so it drives a freshly built
artifact and a library-only change cannot reach it. false when the binary
suite sits in the binary crate's own `tests/`, or is separated only by an
`#[ignore]` or a nextest filter — the tests are still compiled and
collected for every change, so nothing is skipped.
rules.relevance: the repo ships a compiled binary with a subprocess-level end-to-end suite

rules.name: shell_quality_gated
rules.description:
true when both `shellcheck` and `shfmt` run in the gate for every shell
project and fail on issues (no warnings backlog) — as each project's
`lint` and `format` targets, reached by root recipes that delegate to the
orchestrator. false when either is absent from `just check`/CI, is run
advisory-only, or covers only some projects because the root recipe
hand-rolls the list — so a lint or format drift never blocks a merge.

rules.name: target_shell_chosen
rules.description:
true when the target shell is an explicit decision — POSIX `sh` (no bashisms)
or `bash` — declared via a consistent shebang and stated in AGENTS.md, with
the CI matrix matching. false when scripts mix `sh` and `bash` shebangs with
no stated target, so portability is accidental rather than decided.
rules.relevance: the target files are shell scripts or record the shell decision

rules.name: shell_coverage_merged_and_gated
rules.description:
true when the coverage bar is still enforced with the `bats` suite spread
across projects: each project's `test` target writes `kcov`/`bashcov` data
into its declared target outputs, and a repo-level `coverage` target
depending on every `test` merges them (`kcov --merge`, or SimpleCov's
result merging) and fails below the bar — reading the merged line rate
itself, since `kcov` has no fail-under flag. false when the projects' data
is merged but nothing thresholds it, when only one project's coverage is
measured, or when the bar was dropped rather than documented in AGENTS.md
with a reason and still enforced at the lower value.

rules.name: command_surface_wired_uv
rules.description:
true when the root recipes delegate to the orchestrator (`nx affected` /
`nx run-many`) and the projects' targets map the standard work to the
uv-native commands: `bootstrap` -> `uv sync` at the workspace root,
`check` -> the `format`/`lint`/`typecheck`/`test` targets running `ruff
format --check` + `ruff check` + the type checker (`ty`) + `pytest` with
coverage, and `upgrade` -> `uv lock --upgrade`. false when a mapping is
missing, a recipe hand-rolls a per-project loop instead of delegating, or
any of it bypasses uv (bare `pip`, `python -m venv`, a hand-rolled
virtualenv).

rules.name: pyproject_single_source_of_config
rules.description:
true when each project's metadata and tool config live in that project's
`pyproject.toml` alone. false when a committed `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, or
`requirements*.txt` duplicates dependencies or tool config that a
`pyproject.toml` already owns (two sources of truth that drift).

rules.name: coverage_combined_across_projects
rules.description:
true when coverage is measured per project and enforced once over the
union: `[tool.coverage.run]` sets `parallel` and `relative_files`, each
project's `test` target runs `pytest --cov` writing to its own
`COVERAGE_FILE` without a per-project `--cov-fail-under`, and a repo-level
`coverage` target depending on every `test` runs `coverage combine` then
`coverage report --fail-under=<the repo's bar, 95 by default>`, wired into
`just check`. false when the aggregate target is missing so nobody measures
the union, when the threshold is enforced only per project (which cannot
see the lines a sibling e2e project covers), or when the bar was lowered to
accommodate the split rather than the union being measured.

rules.name: toolchain_pinned_and_installed
rules.description:
true when one workspace-root `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the channel and the
components/targets the build needs, and CI installs the toolchain from it
rather than a floating `stable`. false when there is no pinned toolchain
file, a crate carries a competing one, or CI hardcodes a channel that can
drift from the committed pin.

rules.name: dev_profile_and_target_dir
rules.description:
true when the repository root carries `.cargo/config.toml` with
`[build] target-dir = "target"` and `[profile.dev] debug = 1` (the integer
1: line tables only for dev and test builds, `release` untouched), so every
crate in the clone builds into `<clone>/target` and each worktree into its
own. false when the file is missing, either key is absent or holds another
value (`true` is full debuginfo), `target-dir` points outside the clone
(one target directory shared across worktrees), or the keys sit in a
`Cargo.toml` instead of the config file.

rules.name: clippy_denies_warnings
rules.description:
true when the gate runs `clippy` with warnings promoted to errors (`-D
warnings` or an equivalent `deny` config) for every crate — as each
project's `lint` target, reached by root recipes that delegate to the
orchestrator — so a lint is a hard failure anywhere in the workspace. false
when clippy runs warning-only, is absent from the gate, or covers only some
crates because the root recipe hand-rolls the list.

rules.name: coverage_combined_across_crates
rules.description:
true when coverage is measured per project and enforced once over the
union: each project's `test` target runs `cargo llvm-cov --no-report` into
the shared profile directory (declared as that target's outputs) and a
repo-level `coverage` target depending on every `test` runs `cargo llvm-cov
report --fail-under-lines <the repo's bar, 95 by default>`, wired into
`just check`. false when the aggregate target is missing so nobody measures
the union, when `--fail-under-lines` is enforced only per crate (which
cannot see the lines a sibling e2e crate covers), or when the bar was
lowered to accommodate the split.

rules.name: iac_command_surface_wired
rules.description:
true when the root recipes delegate to the orchestrator and the projects'
targets use the Terraform/OpenTofu-native lifecycle: `bootstrap`
initializes the backend in each root module; `check` runs format-check,
validation, tflint, and a security scan per project; and `upgrade`
deliberately updates provider and module constraints plus each root
module's lock file before re-running the gate and reviewing a plan. false
when the surface omits a stage, hand-rolls a per-directory loop instead of
delegating, applies changes from the check recipe, or updates dependencies
without an explicit review step.
rules.relevance: the target files define or invoke the repository command surface for infrastructure work

rules.name: remote_state_policy_wired
rules.description:
true when the repository wires a remote state design with locking, encryption,
access control, recovery, and clear ownership appropriate to its platform,
while ignore policy excludes local state artifacts and `.terraform/`. false
when backend configuration is merely present but its concurrency, sensitivity,
recovery, or ownership model is incomplete or dependent on a developer machine.
rules.relevance: the target files configure or document Terraform/OpenTofu state and repository artifact policy

rules.name: environments_isolated_by_design
rules.description:
true when materially different environments/accounts and independently
operated systems have separate state and deployment units whose boundaries
contain failure and access. false when one mutable workspace or shared state
is the primary isolation mechanism despite different lifecycles, privileges,
or blast-radius needs.
rules.relevance: the target files define or document multiple infrastructure environments, accounts, stacks, or deployment units

rules.name: iac_locks_and_gate_reach_every_unit
rules.description:
true when each root module commits its own `.terraform.lock.hcl` — the
documented exception to one-lockfile-per-ecosystem, since providers resolve
per configuration — while any lint/scan/test harness written in another
language keeps that ecosystem's single root lockfile; AND the gate reaches
every deployment unit, with a repo-level `coverage` target that fails when a
directory containing `*.tf` belongs to no project or a project skipped its
format/validate/lint/scan checks. false when a lock file is uncommitted or
hoisted, or when the split leaves some `*.tf` outside the gate so a full
sweep silently became a partial one.

rules.name: command_surface_wired_bun
rules.description:
true when the root recipes delegate to the orchestrator (`nx affected` /
`nx run-many`) and the projects' targets map the standard work to the
bun-native commands: `bootstrap` -> `bun install` at the workspace root,
`check` -> the `format`/`lint`/`typecheck`/`test` targets running the
format check + lint + `tsc --noEmit` + tests with coverage, and `upgrade`
-> `bun update`. false when a mapping is missing, a recipe hand-rolls a
per-project loop instead of delegating, or any of it bypasses bun (bare
`npm`/`yarn`/`pnpm` with no documented reason).

rules.name: single_lockfile_bun
rules.description:
true when exactly one `bun.lock` (or `bun.lockb`) is committed at the
workspace root, covering every project, and no competing
`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, or `yarn.lock` sits beside it or in
a project subdirectory. false when a second package manager's lockfile is
committed without a documented fallback reason, or a project carries its
own lockfile for the same ecosystem — either way two lockfiles resolve to
different trees.

rules.name: coverage_thresholds_survive_the_split
rules.description:
true when the 95% (or documented lower) coverage bar is still enforced with
the suite spread across projects: every project that has tests sets
`coverageThreshold` in its own `bunfig.toml` (or Vitest
`coverage.thresholds`), OR each project emits LCOV into its declared target
outputs and a repo-level `coverage` target depending on every `test` merges
them and fails below the bar. false when a project shipping code declares
no threshold and feeds no aggregate, so its coverage is measured by nobody,
or when the bar was lowered to accommodate the split.

rules.name: root_commands_delegate
rules.description:
true when each root command recipe shells out to the orchestrator (for example
`nx affected` or `nx run-many`). false when any recipe hand-rolls a
for-each-package loop instead of delegating to the orchestrator.

rules.name: affected_only_explicit_base
rules.description:
true when pull-request CI runs affected-only targets against an explicitly
derived merge base and a full sweep runs on the main branch or nightly.

rules.name: project_boundaries_enforced
rules.description: true when projects declare tags and an enforced allowed-dependency rule.

rules.name: each_deliverable_is_its_own_project
rules.description:
true when every app/package in the repo has its own project definition
declaring its local targets (`build`, `lint`, `test`, `typecheck`) that call
its own language-native tool.

rules.name: graph_splits_by_tier_and_cost
rules.description:
true when the project graph splits the repo's work beyond its deliverables:
the integration and e2e tiers are projects of their own depending on what
they test, and every slow or external-service-touching suite is its own
project depending only on what it tests. The fast unit tier belongs inside
the project whose code it covers. false when the whole repo is one project,
or an expensive suite rides along inside a broadly-depended-on project.

rules.name: graph_splits_by_domain
rules.description:
true when the graph's units are domains — each project holds one concern's
types, interfaces, and logic together — and the only projects several
others depend on are genuine cross-domain contracts. A shared package is a
contract only if adding or changing one domain's concept does not require
editing it. A contract holds what every domain must agree on and never
enumerates the domains: a closed sum type, registry, or table in a central
package with an entry per domain's things is a bag with a type signature,
however it is persisted or served. false when a central project grouped by
kind of code (`types`, `models`, `store`, `data-access`, `utils`, `common`)
sits under every other project, so a change to one domain's concern
rebuilds and re-tests every other; and false when a central project holds
a sum type, registry, or table with an entry per domain, so a domain adding
a concept edits the center and rebuilds every other.
rules.relevance:
the target files declare the workspace's projects, or declare a sum type,
registry, or table that more than one project depends on

rules.name: language_workspace_resolves_dependencies
rules.description:
true when the repo's projects are declared to the language's own workspace
primitive as well as to Nx — a uv workspace, a Cargo workspace, or
bun/pnpm workspaces — with ONE lockfile per language ecosystem covering them
all. false when each project carries its own lockfile for the same ecosystem,
or dependency resolution is hand-wired per project because only Nx knows the
projects exist.
rules.relevance: the repo declares third-party dependencies in a language ecosystem with a workspace primitive

rules.name: no_manual_deploy_step
rules.description:
true when the only human action in a release is merging a PR. false when any
release step requires a manual command, a "Run workflow" click, or hand-editing
a version number.

rules.name: versioning_decoupled_from_building
rules.description:
true when the version job only computes the version and writes the changelog,
manifests, lockfiles, and tag, and a separate workflow builds and publishes on
the tag. false when the version job also builds or publishes artifacts itself.

rules.name: release_job_uses_pat
rules.description:
true when the release or version job authenticates with a PAT or GitHub App
token. false when it authenticates with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (whose tag
push does not fire downstream release or publish workflows).

rules.name: publish_idempotent
rules.description:
true when publishing skips a version that is already live and reads registry
tokens from secrets. false when a re-run would double-publish a version or a
registry token is committed in the tree.
rules.relevance: the repository publishes to a package registry

rules.name: pr_title_conventional_commit_linted
rules.description:
true when a CI job runs on `pull_request` that lints the PR title (the
squash-merge subject the release pipeline reads) against Conventional Commits
— a `commitlint` or equivalent PR-title-lint step. false when no workflow lints
the PR title.

rules.name: broader_sweep_placement_matches_the_release_driver
rules.description:
true when the broader-tier sweep sits where the repo's release driver implies —
at merge-to-main for a push-to-main driver (`semantic-release`, `release-please`
in non-PR mode), where the merged commit is the released commit; on the release PR
for a release-PR gate (`release-plz`, `release-please`), where the commit that
ships is a new commit over a batch of merges. false when a push-to-main repo
sweeps again at release time after sweeping at merge, or a batched repo releases a
commit no job ever swept.

rules.name: plugin_never_calls_asdf
rules.description:
true when no plugin script in the target files invokes `asdf`. false when any
plugin script shells back out to `asdf` (for example `asdf reshim` from
`install`).

rules.name: plugin_split_from_host_tool_integration
rules.description:
true when the plugin project is rooted at the repo root — asdf requires
`bin/` to sit there, so this project alone cannot be moved into a
subdirectory — holding the scripts, any shared `lib/`, and the offline
`bats` tests, while the host-tool integration that installs a real version
over the network is a separate project with its own directory and project
definition, depending on the plugin. false when `asdf plugin test` is a
target of the plugin project itself, so editing a `bats` fixture installs a
real tool version, or when the plugin's `bin/` was relocated to make the
layout uniform and the host tool can no longer find it.

rules.name: asset_naming_contract_shared
rules.description:
true when every install surface that downloads a release asset (an install
script, a Homebrew/Scoop manifest, a CI job) constructs the SAME archive and
`.sha256` name the release workflow produced, from one shared naming scheme.
false when a surface hardcodes an asset name that can drift from what the
release job uploads.
rules.relevance: the repo distributes downloadable release assets across more than one install surface

rules.name: cli_split_from_its_e2e_and_externals
rules.description:
true when the command and its fast unit tests are one project, the suite that
installs and drives the built command is a separate project depending on it,
and each external system the command talks to is its own project carrying its
own live-service suite. false when the subprocess-level suite sits inside the
CLI project — so every change spawns the binary — or when a client for an
external system has no project of its own, so a change to argument parsing
reaches the network.

rules.name: consumer_docs_and_changelog_present
rules.description:
true when the repo ships usage documentation written for a consumer of the
package (how to install and call the public API) and a changelog that records
releases and breaking changes. false when the only docs are internal
development notes.
rules.relevance: the repo ships an installable/consumable package

rules.name: deliverables_and_their_install_suites_split
rules.description:
true when every published package and deployed service is its own project
with its own manifest and fast tests, code shared between them is a project
those consumers depend on, and the suites that install the built artifact or
drive a running service over its real interface are separate projects
depending only on what they exercise. false when several deliverables share
one project, or the install-the-artifact / drive-the-service suite rides
inside the package project, so an unrelated change builds a distributable or
starts a server.

rules.name: next_build_gates_type_and_lint_errors
rules.description:
true when CI runs `next build` and type/lint errors are build blockers — the
Next.js config does not set `typescript.ignoreBuildErrors` or
`eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds` to silence them. false when the production build is
never run in CI, or errors are configured away so a broken build ships.

rules.name: react_hooks_lint_rules_enabled
rules.description:
true when the lint config enables the Rules of Hooks and the effect
dependency check — `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` with `rules-of-hooks` and
`exhaustive-deps` as errors, or the Biome equivalents (`useHookAtTopLevel`,
`useExhaustiveDependencies`). false when neither is configured, so hook
misuse and stale-closure effect bugs pass the gate.
rules.relevance: the target files configure the JS/TS linter

rules.name: feature_import_boundaries_enforced_at_both_scopes
rules.description:
true when the unidirectional feature-import architecture is enforced at both
scopes it spans: inside an app project by the linter — an
`import/no-restricted-paths` (ESLint) or `noRestrictedImports` (Biome) rule
banning cross-feature internal imports and shared code importing from
features — and between projects by the orchestrator's module-boundary tag
rule, so a second app cannot reach into the first's `src/` instead of
depending on a shared UI project. false when either scope is unenforced,
leaving the shared → features → app boundary to convention where it is
easiest to cross.
rules.relevance: the target files configure the JS/TS linter's import rules or the project boundary tags

rules.name: validate_and_smoke_every_skill_gated
rules.description:
true when `just check` both validates every `SKILL.md` (frontmatter,
forbidden runtime deps) and SMOKE-runs every bundled script once, so a broken
skill fails the gate. false when validation/smoke exists but is not wired into
`check`, or only a subset of skills is covered.

rules.name: own_checks_dogfooded
rules.description:
true when any repo-baseline or lint script the repo itself ships is run
against this repo inside `just check`, so the canonical example stays passing.
false when the repo authors such a check but never runs it on itself.
rules.relevance: the repo ships its own baseline/lint tooling

rules.name: one_project_per_skill
rules.description:
true when each skill directory is its own project declaring the same target
names as every other skill (`validate`, `smoke`, `test`, plus the repo's
uniform `lint`/`format`), so `nx affected -t test` fans out by name and
editing one skill runs that skill's targets rather than the whole catalog,
and the shared validation tooling is its own project the skill projects
depend on. false when the catalog is one project — so any skill edit runs
every skill's targets — or when skills invent different target names, which
makes a single fan-out reach only some of them.

rules.name: skill_project_edges_are_authoring_only
rules.description:
true when the dependency a skill project declares on the shared validation
tooling exists purely to order and cache authoring targets, while the
bundled scripts themselves remain self-contained. false when that project
edge is mirrored by a real runtime import — a bundled script importing the
repo's tooling, or relying on the orchestrator to run — which breaks the
scripts inside a consuming repo where none of it exists.

rules.name: production_build_validated_in_ci
rules.description:
true when CI builds the PRODUCTION bundle (not just starts the dev server) and
treats type and lint errors as build blockers. false when CI only runs the dev
server or tests, so a production build could be broken and merge anyway.

rules.name: app_browser_suite_and_services_split
rules.description:
true when the app and its fast unit/component tests are one project, the
browser suite is its own project whose `test` target depends on the app's
`build`, and each backend service the app calls is its own project rather
than a directory inside the app. false when the browser suite lives in the
app project — so any change can start a browser — or when a backend service
is a folder of the app project, so a server-only change rebuilds the frontend
and vice versa.

rules.name: live_tier_compiles_and_requires_credential
rules.description:
true when every test in the tier stays compiled (never `#[cfg]`'d out or
deleted) and the workflow requires the credential, failing fast with a clear
message when it is absent. false when a test is excluded from compilation, or
the workflow skips or no-ops to a green pass without the credential —
reporting the tier as covered when it never ran.
rules.relevance: the target files define a live or integration test tier

rules.name: no_untrusted_interpolation_in_run
rules.description:
when a workflow reads untrusted event data (`${{ github.event.* }}` — a PR title,
body, branch name, or comment) only by binding it to an `env:` variable and then
referencing that variable inside `run:` (e.g. `env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}`
then `run: echo "$TITLE"`), never by expanding `${{ github.event.* }}` literally in
the `run:` script text. Event data mapped into `env:`, `with:`, `if:`, or an action's
inputs is compliant — only a `${{ github.event.* }}` expansion written directly in a
`run:` block, where a crafted value is parsed as shell, is a violation.
rules.relevance: the target files define a GitHub Actions workflow with a `run:` step

rules.name: ci_invokes_gate_recipe_not_inline_stages
rules.description:
true when a workflow job that runs the quality gate invokes the project's single
gate recipe (e.g. `just check`) rather than re-listing its individual stages
(format check, lint, type check, unit tests, e2e) as inline commands. false when a
job reimplements gate stages inline, so the gate CI runs can silently drift out of
parity with the one a contributor runs locally. A job that legitimately runs
something outside the gate (a separate install-smoke, live-test, or release job) is
not a violation.
rules.relevance: the target files define a CI job that runs the quality gate

rules.name: external_service_suite_stays_out_of_the_affected_tier
rules.description:
true when every such suite runs from its own credential-gated workflow or a
target promoted out of the affected tier, rather than from the affected-tier
gate a pull request runs. false when a change wires one into the PR gate —
including a fast one, since that promotion is decided by what the suite
touches, not by how long it takes.
rules.relevance: the target files wire a test suite that contacts an external service

rules.name: no_second_broader_sweep_over_an_already_gated_commit
rules.description:
true when no job runs the broader-tier sweep (a full `run-many` over every
project, or the same gating targets) against a commit another job already swept —
the same SHA, or a different SHA over an identical tree, such as a tag build or a
release-prep job following the merge that swept it. false when a workflow adds a
second sweep of an already-swept commit, e.g. a release, tag, or publish workflow
re-running lint, type-check, or tests over the commit merge-to-main already swept.
Building or publishing an artifact from a swept commit is not gating and is not a
violation; neither is the first sweep of a squash-merge commit, whose tree is new.
rules.relevance: the target files define a job that runs gating targets (lint, type-check, tests, or a full sweep)

rules.name: robust_shell
rules.description:
true when `set -euo pipefail` is set, every expansion is quoted, and network
and filesystem failures are handled explicitly. false when `set -euo pipefail`
is omitted, an expansion is unquoted, or an operation is assumed to succeed.

rules.name: portable_to_target_shell
rules.description:
when every construct stays within the declared target shell and avoids
non-portable operations (`sort -V`, bashisms under POSIX `sh`) the declared
shell or platform does not support.

rules.name: shell_test_tiers_stay_split
rules.description:
true when it lives in the project whose cost it matches — the offline
behaviour tests in the script project, and any suite that drives a real
host tool, installs a real version, or reaches the network in a separate
project depending only on the scripts it exercises. false when a network-
or host-tool-touching test is added to the offline project, so every
unrelated script edit pays for it, or when an env-var guard skips it at
runtime in place of moving it out of the fast project. A guard that skips
because a credential or host tool the suite genuinely requires is absent
is a capability check, not a tier, and is not a violation.
rules.relevance: the target files add or change a shell test suite, or the project definition that owns one

rules.name: async_typed_clients_at_boundaries
rules.description:
true when every external network or IO service uses an async, typed client (an
official typed client, or a small typed async client written for the repo).
false when any such call uses an untyped or synchronous ad-hoc client.
rules.relevance: the target files call an external network or IO service

rules.name: structural_pattern_matching
rules.description:
true when multi-branch dispatch on one subject's shape, type, or value uses
`match`/`case` with destructuring where that reads more clearly than an if/elif
chain. false when an if/elif chain repeats `isinstance`, index, or attribute
checks on that subject where `match`/`case` would express it directly.
rules.relevance: the target files dispatch on the shape, type, or value of a subject

rules.name: modern_domain_modeling
rules.description:
true when structured data in the target files is modelled with dataclasses,
enums, `NamedTuple`, or typed models (e.g. Pydantic), and a meaningful
primitive (id, token) uses a `NewType` or type alias. false when structured
data is passed around as bare dicts, positional tuples, or stringly-typed
constants where a typed model or enum is the natural choice.
rules.relevance: the target files define or pass around structured domain data

rules.name: protocol_based_seams
rules.description:
true when a pluggable dependency or seam in the target files is typed with a
`typing.Protocol` so callers depend on the structural interface. false when a
seam meant to be swappable is bound to a concrete class or a heavyweight
nominal ABC where a `Protocol` fits.
rules.relevance: the target files define a pluggable dependency or seam

rules.name: no_injection_from_untrusted_input
rules.description:
when the target files keep untrusted input out of dangerous sinks: no `shell=True`
on externally-influenced input, no `eval`/`exec` or unsafe deserialization
(`pickle.loads`, `yaml.load` without `SafeLoader`) of untrusted data, and SQL and
OS commands built with parameterized APIs rather than string interpolation.
rules.relevance: the target files run subprocesses, execute dynamic code, deserialize data, or build SQL or OS commands

rules.name: projects_stay_in_one_uv_workspace
rules.description:
true when every Python distribution is a member of the root uv workspace
(`[tool.uv.workspace] members`), carries its own `pyproject.toml`, depends on
sibling distributions through `[tool.uv.sources] workspace = true`, and
resolves against the single root `uv.lock` — a repo with exactly one
distribution, at the repo root, needs no `[tool.uv.workspace]` table.
false when a distribution is invisible to the workspace, commits a second
`uv.lock`/`requirements.txt` for the same ecosystem, or reaches a sibling's
source by a relative path import instead of a declared workspace dependency.
rules.relevance: the target files add or change the manifest, lock, or project definition of a Python distribution — a unit that owns Python source together with its own dependency set, not a build-graph project that only declares targets run over source rooted elsewhere in the workspace

rules.name: test_tiers_split_by_project_not_by_marker
rules.description:
true when it lives in its own project whose `test` target runs it, so `nx
affected` can skip it. false when the tier is expressed as a pytest marker
the default run deselects (`-m "not slow"`, `addopts` with a deselecting
`-m`, or a skip keyed off an env var) while the tests stay inside the fast
project — which hides the cost instead of removing it. A guard that skips
because a credential or provider the suite genuinely requires is absent is
a capability check, not a tier, and is not a violation.
rules.relevance: the target files add or change a pytest suite that is slow or reaches an external service, or the marker configuration that selects one

rules.name: invalid_states_unrepresentable
rules.description:
true when the domain and boundary types in the target files use newtypes and
enums so that invalid states cannot be represented. false when any domain or
boundary value is modelled with a bare bool or a stringly-typed value where a
newtype or enum is the natural choice.
rules.relevance: the target files define domain types or model boundary data

rules.name: no_panics_on_recoverable_errors
rules.description:
true when every fallible operation in the target files returns or propagates an
error (`Result`, `?`). false when any fallible operation uses `unwrap()`,
`expect()`, or `panic!` for an error that is recoverable.
rules.relevance: the target files perform fallible operations

rules.name: crates_stay_in_one_cargo_workspace
rules.description:
true when every crate in the repo is a `[workspace] members` entry of the
root virtual manifest, inherits its shared metadata and dependency versions
(`rust-version.workspace = true`, `serde = { workspace = true }`), depends
on sibling crates as path/workspace dependencies, and resolves against the
single root `Cargo.lock` and the single workspace-root
`rust-toolchain.toml`. false when a crate is invisible to the workspace,
commits its own `Cargo.lock` or `rust-toolchain.toml`, or pins a dependency
version the workspace already pins. A repo with exactly one crate at the
repo root needs no `[workspace]` table to be true — the claim is that no
crate resolves outside the one root lock.
rules.relevance: the target files add or change a crate's manifest, lock, toolchain pin, or project definition

rules.name: state_backend_discipline
rules.description:
true when state ownership, locking, encryption, access control, and recovery
form a coherent remote-backend design for the target infrastructure. false
when state depends on a developer machine, has ambiguous ownership, or lacks
a credible concurrency or recovery strategy.
rules.relevance: the target files define or configure infrastructure state or deployment stacks

rules.name: cohesive_blast_radius_boundaries
rules.description:
true when modules/stacks have cohesive responsibilities and small interfaces,
while environments and independently operated systems are separated into
state and deployment units sized to contain failures. false when unrelated
resources share a convenience module or one state/deployment unit couples
environments or systems with independent lifecycles.
rules.relevance: the target files define modules, stacks, environments, or deployment boundaries

rules.name: secrets_avoid_code_and_state
rules.description:
true when secret material is referenced from a managed secret store at
deployment time, secret-bearing interfaces are marked sensitive, and the
design avoids persisting plaintext secrets in state. false when credentials
are supplied as literals or ordinary inputs/outputs, or sensitivity marking
is treated as protection against a secret being stored in state.
rules.relevance: the target files create, consume, pass, or expose credentials or other secret material

rules.name: declarative_drift_resistant_resources
rules.description:
true when desired state is expressed with native resources and lifecycle or
import choices preserve reconciliation. false when imperative provisioners,
`local-exec`, `null_resource`, timing, or broad ignored-change rules replace
an available resource model or conceal meaningful drift.
rules.relevance: the target files provision or manage infrastructure resources or their lifecycle

rules.name: stable_resource_addressing
rules.description:
true when repeated resources use stable domain identities, choosing keyed
iteration such as `for_each` when insertion or reordering must not re-address
existing instances. false when positional `count` or generated indices make
ordinary collection edits replace or rename unrelated resources.
rules.relevance: the target files create repeated or collection-derived infrastructure resources

rules.name: legible_names_tags_and_dependencies
rules.description:
true when stable names and tags/labels communicate ownership, environment,
service, and applicable cost or compliance intent, and dependencies follow
real data flow through references/outputs. false when generic naming obscures
operational intent, metadata is inconsistent, or incidental ordering stands
in for a real dependency (with explicit dependency metadata reserved for
dependencies the provider cannot infer).
rules.relevance: the target files name, tag, label, or connect infrastructure resources

rules.name: least_privilege_policy_intent
rules.description:
true when IAM and resource policies grant only the actions, resources,
principals, and conditions justified by the workload, with any broad grant
carrying a concrete constraint or migration rationale. false when authority
is broader than the workload requires even if the policy is syntactically
valid and passes a deterministic security scanner.
rules.relevance: the target files define or assemble IAM, identity, trust, or resource policies

rules.name: deliberate_provider_module_versions
rules.description:
true when provider and external-module constraints prevent silent unreviewed
changes while retaining a practical reviewed upgrade path, and unusually
broad, narrow, or source-ref constraints have a recorded reason. false when
constraints float without review intent or freeze dependencies indefinitely
without explaining the tradeoff.
rules.relevance: the target files select, source, or constrain an infrastructure provider, module, construct, or component

rules.name: every_deployment_unit_is_a_project
rules.description:
true when it is its own project with a project definition beside its
configuration, and a stack consuming a shared module declares that edge
(via the `source` path the orchestrator can infer, or
`implicitDependencies`) so a module change marks exactly its consumers
affected. false when a new root module is added with no project definition
— leaving it outside the gate entirely — or when a consumed shared module
is not an edge, so either every stack plans on any module edit or none of
them do.
rules.relevance: the target files add or change a root module, a reusable module, or the project definition that owns one

rules.name: no_unjustified_any_or_non_null
rules.description:
when every use of `any` or a non-null assertion (`!`) in the target files
carries a comment justifying why the type system is bypassed.
rules.relevance: the target files use `any` or a non-null assertion

rules.name: projects_stay_in_one_js_workspace
rules.description:
true when every TypeScript project in the repo is a member of the root
workspace (the root `package.json` `workspaces` array, or
`pnpm-workspace.yaml`), carries its own `package.json` and `tsconfig.json`,
depends on sibling projects by package name with the `workspace:*` protocol,
and resolves against the single root lockfile. false when a project is
invisible to the workspace, commits a second lockfile for the same
ecosystem, or reaches a sibling through a deep relative path
(`../other-project/src/...`) instead of a declared workspace dependency. A
repo with exactly one project, rooted at the repo root, needs no
`workspaces` array to be true — the claim is that no project resolves
outside the one root lock.
rules.relevance: the target files add or change a TypeScript project's manifest, tsconfig, lock, or project definition

rules.name: instruction_layer_localized
rules.description:
true when subtree rules live in a nested `AGENTS.md` inside each project,
leaving the root `AGENTS.md` to repo-wide constraints only. false when
project-specific rules are piled into the root `AGENTS.md`.

rules.name: expensive_tests_stay_behind_their_own_edge
rules.description:
true when the test lives in a project whose graph edges reach only what it
actually tests, so an unrelated change cannot make it run. false when it sits
in a broadly-depended-on project, or its project depends on unrelated code
(an import, a `dependsOn`, or an implicit dependency), so every change in the
repo pays for it.
rules.relevance:
the target files add or change a test that is slow or reaches an external
service (a live API, a container, a browser, a real database), or change the
project definition that owns one

rules.name: new_projects_keep_the_graph_uniform
rules.description:
true when the project declares the repo's standard target names for the work
it has (`build`, `lint`, `test`, `typecheck`) and the boundary tags its layer
requires, so `nx affected`/`run-many` fan out by name and the module-boundary
rule can judge it. false when it invents a target name the repo already names,
omits a target it has work for, or is untagged where its layer is tag-enforced.
rules.relevance: the target files declare a project that did not exist before

rules.name: code_lands_in_the_domain_that_owns_it
rules.description:
true when a new or changed type, interface (a trait, protocol, abstract base,
or port), store or repository interface, or helper lands in the project of
the domain that owns it — the project whose other code changes when that
concern changes — or in a project that is a genuine cross-domain contract: a
shared identity, an envelope or representation rule, a wire or storage
format, or an interface every domain must agree on. A shared package is a
contract only if adding or changing one domain's concept does not require
editing it. A contract holds what every domain must agree on and never
enumerates the domains: a closed sum type, registry, or table in a central
package with an entry per domain's things is a bag with a type signature,
however it is persisted or served. false when it lands in a project grouped
by the kind of code it is rather than by the concern it serves — a central
`types`, `models`, `store`, `data-access`, `utils`, `common` or `shared`
package several domains depend on — so that a change to one domain's concern
re-touches a package every other domain builds against; and false when it
adds one domain's entry — a variant, a registration, a row, a case — to a
closed sum type, registry, or table in a central package, or declares one
domain's structs in the central package because a central enumeration
reaches them. The project's name is a signal, not the test: a `types`
project holding only the identities, the envelope and the formats every
domain agrees on is a contract, and a `contract` project holding one
domain's structs beside another's is a bag.
rules.relevance:
the change adds, moves, or re-homes a type, interface, store or repository
interface, or helper declaration; adds a variant, registration, row, or
case to a sum type, registry, or table shared across projects; or gives one
project a dependency on another. A change confined to the body of an
existing function inside one project is not judged

rules.name: release_does_not_regate_an_already_swept_commit
rules.description:
true when it only computes the version, writes the changelog and manifests,
builds, and publishes — running no lint, type-check, or test target over a
commit the merge (or the release PR) already swept with the broader tier.
Compiling the artifact it ships is building, not gating, and is not a
violation.
rules.relevance: the target files define a release, tag, or publish workflow

rules.name: safe_pinned_downloads
rules.description:
true when every download in the target files pins an exact HTTPS version URL
and either verifies a published checksum or uses an atomic `.part` download,
cleaning up temp files on failure. false when any download uses a mutable
`latest` URL, skips checksum verification without an atomic download, or leaves
partial files behind on failure.
rules.relevance: the target files download a file

rules.name: portable_version_handling
rules.description:
when version sorting in the target files uses a portable comparator (never
`sort -V`) and normalizes OS and arch names portably.
rules.relevance: the target files sort versions or normalize OS or arch names

rules.name: plugin_scripts_stay_at_the_contract_path
rules.description:
true when it stays in the repo-root `bin/` the host tool looks in,
belonging to the plugin project whose root is therefore the repo root,
with shared helpers in `lib/` beside it. false when a plugin script is
moved into a subdirectory to make the layout look like the other projects
— asdf resolves `bin/` relative to the plugin repo root, so the plugin
silently stops working — or when a non-plugin concern is added to `bin/`,
where asdf will treat it as part of the contract.
rules.relevance: the target files add, move, or remove a script asdf invokes, or the project definition that owns them

rules.name: cli_output_contract
rules.description:
true when the CLI uses distinct, documented exit codes (`0` only on success),
writes error messages to stderr, and keeps machine-readable output (e.g.
`--json`) separate from human prose. false when the CLI conflates exit codes,
prints errors to stdout, or mixes machine-readable output with human prose.
rules.relevance: the target files implement CLI output or exit-code handling

rules.name: new_command_or_client_gets_its_own_project
rules.description:
true when it arrives as its own project — so `nx affected` can run it
alone and its live-service suite stays out of reach of unrelated changes.
false when a second command is folded into the existing CLI project as
another entry point, or an external-system client is added inside it,
making every change to argument parsing pay for that command's tests and
its network calls.
rules.relevance: the target files add a command the tool exposes, or a client for an external system it calls

rules.name: stable_public_surface
rules.description:
true when the target files mark what is public versus internal (explicit
exports, `__all__`, or visibility modifiers) so the public API is intentional.
false when internal implementation is exposed in the public surface with no
public/internal distinction.
rules.relevance: the target files define part of the package's public API

rules.name: shared_internals_are_a_project_not_a_reach_in
rules.description:
true when that code lives in a project of its own that each consumer
declares a dependency on. false when one package reaches into another's
internals — a relative path import across package directories, or a
re-export of a sibling's private module — so the graph shows no edge where
a real coupling exists and affected detection cannot see it.
rules.relevance: the target files share implementation code between two packages or services in this repo

rules.name: server_input_validated_with_schema
rules.description:
true when every Route Handler and Server Action in the target files validates
its input (request body, form data, search params) with a runtime schema (e.g.
Zod) before using it. false when a handler or action trusts `unknown`/`any`
input from the request directly, so malformed or hostile input reaches the
server logic unchecked.
rules.relevance: the target files define a Next.js Route Handler or Server Action

rules.name: features_do_not_cross_import
rules.description:
true when no module under `src/features/<A>` imports from another feature's
internals (`src/features/<B>/...`); features are composed only at the
routes/app layer or through shared top-level modules. false when a feature
module reaches directly into another feature's internal files, coupling the
two and breaking the unidirectional shared → features → app flow.
rules.relevance: the target files live inside a feature module

rules.name: server_state_not_duplicated_in_global_store
rules.description:
true when server-fetched data is owned by a data-fetching/query layer (e.g.
TanStack Query, RTK Query) and read from there. false when data fetched from
the server is copied into a global client store (Redux/Zustand/Context) as
the source of truth, so the store and the server can drift out of sync.
rules.relevance: the target files fetch server data or define a global client store

rules.name: stateful_logic_extracted_to_hooks
rules.description:
true when a component's data-fetching, mutations, subscriptions, and
non-trivial derived state live in custom hooks (`useX`), leaving the
component body mostly declarative markup that wires hook results to JSX.
false when a component inlines substantial business logic — fetching,
effects, and branching orchestration — beside its render instead of
extracting it into a hook.
rules.relevance: the target files define a React component

rules.name: feature_code_colocated
rules.description:
true when a feature's components, hooks, API calls, state, and types live
together under its own app project's `src/features/<feature>/`. false when
code belonging to one feature is scattered across that project's global
type-based folders (a top-level `components/`, `hooks/`, or `services/`)
instead of being colocated with its feature, so no directory owns the
feature end to end.
rules.relevance: the target files belong to a feature that should be colocated

rules.name: dangerous_html_is_sanitized
rules.description:
true when every `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` is fed HTML that is constant or
sanitized (e.g. via DOMPurify) before rendering. false when user-supplied or
other untrusted content is passed to `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` without
sanitization, opening an XSS hole.
rules.relevance: the target files render `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`

rules.name: shared_ui_graduates_to_its_own_project
rules.description:
true when it lives in a shared UI project that each app depends on. false
when a second app consumes it by importing across app-project boundaries —
a relative path into another app's `src/`, or a deep import past a
project's public entry point — instead of graduating it into a project of
its own, which couples the two apps without an edge the graph or the
module-boundary rule can see.
rules.relevance: the target files share a component, hook, or utility between two apps in this repo

rules.name: scripts_runtime_independent
rules.description:
when every bundled skill script in the target files is self-contained (PEP 723
inline metadata for Python, Node built-ins for JavaScript) and depends on no
orchestrator, repo-root manifest or lockfile, asdf or direnv, or import from the
repo's own source tree.

rules.name: determinism_vs_judgment
rules.description:
true when the deterministic steps described in the target files are implemented
as scripts and prose is reserved for genuine judgment. false when a SKILL.md or
AGENTS.md narrates step-by-step deterministic actions that a script should own.
rules.relevance: the target files describe procedural steps

rules.name: skill_description_trigger_and_compatibility_needs
rules.description:
true when every SKILL.md `description` in the target files is trigger-oriented
(states when to use the skill, e.g. "Use when …") and `compatibility` states
the skill's real runtime needs. false when any description is a vague title or
omits real runtime needs.

rules.name: each_skill_is_its_own_project
rules.description:
true when that directory has its own project definition, so `nx affected`
runs that skill's targets and leaves the rest of the catalog alone, and an
expensive harness-driving eval it ships sits in a project of its own.
false when a skill is added with no project definition — leaving it
outside the graph, so editing it either runs the whole catalog or nothing
— or when its slow eval is declared as another target of the skill's own
project, making every edit to that skill pay for a real harness run.
rules.relevance: the target files add, move, or restructure a skill directory

rules.name: secrets_stay_server_side
rules.description:
true when secrets and privileged data access stay in server-only code and only
non-sensitive data crosses to the client. false when a secret or a privileged
data-access path is reachable from client code.
rules.relevance: the target files handle secrets or privileged data access

rules.name: authorization_enforced_server_side
rules.description:
when every privileged action or data-access path in the target files verifies
authentication and authorization on the server before acting — a control hidden in
the UI is never the only guard.
rules.relevance: the target files expose a server route, action, or data-access path

rules.name: url_state_validated
rules.description: when shareable state kept in the URL is parsed and validated before use.
rules.relevance: the target files read shareable state from the URL

rules.name: e2e_uses_accessible_selectors
rules.description:
true when every end-to-end test in the target files selects elements by
accessible role or user-facing text. false when any end-to-end test selects
elements by a brittle CSS or DOM selector.
rules.relevance: the target files define end-to-end tests that select page elements

rules.name: browser_journeys_run_against_the_built_app
rules.description:
true when the spec lives in the app's separate e2e project, whose `test`
target depends on the app's `build`, so the journey drives the production
bundle. false when a browser journey is added inside the app project
itself — where every unrelated change pays to start a browser — or when
the e2e project drives a development server instead of the built artifact,
so the bundle users receive is never the one exercised.
rules.relevance: the target files add or change a browser-driven end-to-end journey, or the project definition that owns one

rules.name: budget_descriptions_durable_and_terse
rules.description:
true when each budget's `description` says, in one or two sentences, what is
measured and what it protects. false when a description reads as session or
changelog narrative — base figures from an old commit, a history of the
figure, or what each journey did — or restates the budget's own fields: its
command, unit, direction or threshold.
rules.relevance: the target file declares a budget with a `description`

rules.name: budgets_scoped_to_minimal_tree
rules.description:
true when everything specific to a `budgets.yaml`'s measurements lives in the
tree that file's directory roots: the commands it names, the tests they run,
and budget-only fixtures. Calling shared code that lives elsewhere is fine —
a common harness, the code under measurement, a fixture other tests also
use, or telemetry recording added to an existing test or runtime code. false
only when something that exists solely to serve one of its budgets
lives outside that tree.
rules.relevance:
the target file declares budgets, or is a script, test or fixture that a
budget's `command` runs or reads

rules.name: onebudgetspec_is_the_only_judge
rules.description:
true when the code a budget's `command` runs reports its figure (to the file
`ONEBUDGETSPEC_RESULT` names, or as its elapsed run) and leaves the comparison
with the threshold to onebudgetspec. false when that code reads a
`budgets.yaml`, or asserts the figure against a threshold itself.
rules.relevance:
the target file declares budgets, or is code a budget's `command` runs to
produce its figure

rules.name: budget_commands_measure_directly
rules.description:
true when each budget's `command` runs its measurement directly, or through
one generic runner shared by every budget. false when it goes through a
per-budget wrapper that re-lists budget ids or re-checks that a result was
written — work onebudgetspec already does.
rules.relevance:
the target file declares budgets, or is a script or program a budget's
`command` names

rules.name: budgets_reuse_gate_telemetry
rules.description:
true when a budget whose behaviour an existing gate's tests or runtime already
exercise takes its figure from telemetry those runs record and save
temporarily (for example as the test target's output), its `command` only
analysing that data. Also true when no existing gate exercises the measured
behaviour, or when recording it there would cost more than a standalone
measurement. false when a budget re-runs a scenario an existing test already
runs, only to count or time it, where adding telemetry to that test or its
runtime code would be cheaper than the extra gate time.
rules.relevance:
the target file declares budgets, or is code a budget's `command` runs, or a
test exercising behaviour a budget measures

rules.name: tests_hold_no_nonfunctional_thresholds
rules.description:
false when the file asserts a cost figure against a fixed bound — wall
clock, request, query or API-point count, payload or artifact size, memory
or money at a realistic workload — or tells two behaviours apart by elapsed
time ("returned within 2 s, so it did not wait") rather than asserting the
observable event. true otherwise, including a configured timeout, deadline
or backoff asserted near its value, an exact count of an action, the
absence of an operation, a limit the product itself enforces, and a timeout
that only guards against a hang.
rules.relevance:
the target file is test code (a test file, or a Rust file with a
`#[cfg(test)]` module) that asserts, measures or records a timing, size or
count figure, reads the clock, or bounds a wait with a timeout

rules.name: budgets_track_product_owner_outcomes
rules.description:
Budgets track product-owner outcomes, with finer figures as their breakdown.
false when the file registers a budget whose figure is a part of another
budget's figure the repository registers — a step, phase or operation of it
— or the same concern as another budget in a second unit, such as requests
beside points for one quota. true otherwise. Whether a product owner would
care about a figure is never judged.
rules.relevance: the target file declares budgets
